'''''Zantedeschia aethiopica''''', commonly known as '''calla lily''', '''arum lily''', and '''death lily''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Araceae]], native to [[southern Africa]] in [[Lesotho]], [[South Africa]], and [[Eswatini]].<ref name="grin">{{GRIN | access-date = 2017-12-18}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Jarro-2.jpg|thumb|Inflorescence and spathe]]
''Zantedeschia aethiopica'' is a [[Rhizome|rhizomatous]] [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]], [[evergreen]] where rainfall and temperatures are adequate, [[deciduous]] where there is a [[dry season]]. Its preferred habitat is in or on the banks of streams and ponds. It grows to {{convert|0.6|–|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with large clumps of broad, arrow shaped dark green [[leaf|leaves]] up to {{convert|45|cm|in|abbr=on}} long. The [[inflorescence]]s are large and are produced in spring, summer and autumn, with a pure white [[spathe]] up to {{convert|25|cm|in|abbr=on}} and a yellow [[spadix (botany)|spadix]] up to {{convert|9|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=rhs>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref> The spadix produces a faint, sweet fragrance.<ref>{{Cite web|url= https://pza.sanbi.org/zantedeschia-aethiopica|title=Zantedeschia aethiopica|website=SANBI PlantZAfrica.com|access-date=2022-06-27}}</ref>

''Zantedeschia aethiopica'' contains [[calcium oxalate]], and ingestion of the raw plant may cause a severe burning sensation and swelling of lips, tongue, and throat; stomach pain and diarrhea may occur.<ref>[http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/poison/Zanteae.htm Poisonous Plants of North Carolina] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130903111246/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/poison/Zanteae.htm |date=2013-09-03 }} Retrieved on 8-2-2009</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Zantedeschia+aethiopica|title=''Zantedeschia aethiopica''|website=www.pfaf.org|access-date=2017-01-31}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Z. aethiopica'' is native to [[southern Africa]], specifically [[Lesotho]], [[Mozambique]], [[South Africa]], and [[Eswatini]]. It has [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in [[Kenya]], [[Madeira]], [[Azores]], [[Malawi]], [[New Zealand]], [[Tanzania]], [[Zambia]], coastal [[California]], in western Europe from the [[Iberian Peninsula]] to [[Ireland]], the high altitude mountainous areas of Luzon in the [[Philippines]], and [[Australia]], particularly in [[Western Australia]] where it has been classified as a toxic weed and pest.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=H10|title= Arum Lily|access-date= 2008-04-23|work= Weeds Australia Weed identification|archive-date= 2008-04-16|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080416222515/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=H10}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://agspsrv95.agric.wa.gov.au/dps/version02/01_plantview.asp?page=1&contentID=7&|title=Arum lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica)|access-date=2008-04-23|work=Declared plant in Western Australia|archive-date=2008-07-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080719061114/http://agspsrv95.agric.wa.gov.au/dps/version02/01_plantview.asp?page=1&contentID=7&}} [[Department of Agriculture and Food (Western Australia)|Dept Agriculture and Food]], Western Australia</ref> The majority of invasive populations are located in coastal prairies and [[wetlands]] near human settlements.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Zantedeschia aethiopica Profile – California Invasive Plant Council |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/zantesdeschia-aethiopica-profile/ |access-date=2023-02-25 |language=en-US}}</ref> It is also a highly [[invasive species]] in [[Riparian zone|riparian zones]] and pastureland of Western Australia and New Zealand.<ref name=":0" /> The [[cultivar]] 'Green Goddess' is listed in the New Zealand [[National Pest Plant Accord]], which proscribes its cultivation, sale, and distribution. 

The reproduction of ''Z. aethiopica'' involves [[Seed dispersal|seeds dispersal]] by birds and [[vegetative propagation]] through [[rhizomes]] that can spread when soil or garden cuttings are moved.<ref name=":0" />

== Cultivation and uses ==
A number of [[cultivar]]s have been selected as [[ornamental plant]]s:

* 'Crowborough' is a more cold tolerant cultivar growing to {{convert|90|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall, suited to cool climates, such as Ireland or Britain and the north-western [[United States]].{{citation needed|date=September 2013}}
* 'Green Goddess' has green stripes on the spathes which allow the flowers to last much longer than the original white form. 'Green Goddess' also has a more opened and wider spathe and has the tendency to develop curvy fringes at the edge of the spathe than the original white form. The first generation hybrid of 'Green Goddess' and the original white form have a light green underside on the spathe, allowing the flower to last longer than the original white form, but no green stripes on the top side.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}} The New Zealand National Pest Plant Accord proscribes the cultivation, sale, and distribution of 'Green Goddess'.
* 'Pink Mist' has a pinkish base to the spathe and pink spadix. 'Pink Mist' is not a hybrid, but a colour sport. The pink colour is best developed in partial shade after rain. 'Pink Mist' is quite delicate and weak compared to the original white form and 'Green Goddess'. Unlike the latter, 'Pink Mist' has a dormant period during winter, where the leaves almost die down completely, although it is pure ''Z. aethiopica''. The seedlings of 'Pink Mist' are also weaker than the original white form or 'Green Goddess'.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}}
* 'Red Desire' has a red instead of yellow spadix and appears to be very rare.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}}
* 'White Sail', growing to 90 cm tall, has a very broad spathe.<ref name=rhs/>

The cultivars 'Crowborough'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/89813/Zantedeschia-aethiopica-Crowborough/Details | title = ''Zantedeschia aethiopica'' 'Crowborough' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> and 'Green Goddess'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/60961/Zantedeschia-aethiopica-Green-Goddess/Details | title = ''Zantedeschia aethiopica'' 'Green Goddess' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 108 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 11 March 2019}}</ref>

In order to introduce colours to the large white calla lilies, like the many colours available in the dwarf summer calla lilies, attempts have been made to hybridise ''Z. aethiopica'' with ''Z. elliotiana''. These have resulted in albino progeny, which are non-viable.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}}

''Zantedeschia aethiopica'' can be used for treatment of wastewater due to its tolerance of iron and ability to grow in wet areas.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Casierra-Posada|first1=Fánor|last2=Blanke|first2=Michael M.|last3=Guerrero-Guío|first3=Juan Carlos|date=June 2014|title=Iron Tolerance in Calla Lilies (''Zantedeschia aethiopica'')|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10343-014-0316-y|journal=Gesunde Pflanzen|language=en|volume=66|issue=2|pages=63–68|doi=10.1007/s10343-014-0316-y|s2cid=9473100|issn=0367-4223|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Symbolism ==
Until 2011, ''Zantedeschia aethiopica'' was the national flower of the island nation of [[Saint Helena]], where it grows widely, but is considered an invasive plant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Flower ⋅ Saint Helena Island Info ⋅ About St Helena, in the South Atlantic Ocean |url=http://sainthelenaisland.info/nationalflower.htm |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=sainthelenaisland.info}}</ref> Further, it is an important symbol of [[Irish republicanism]] and [[Irish nationalism|nationalism]] since 1926, because it is used to commemorate the dead of [[Easter Rising|Easter 1916]] and onward.{{citation needed|date=September 2013}}
